posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md: Heck, I have never used that stuff and I have never had emulsion lift off my glass...ever. Is there something different in the silver process that makes it less adhesive to CLEAN glass?

posts.author: jean
posts.content_md:
> **JohnFP:** Heck, I have never used that stuff and I have never had emulsion lift off my glass...ever. Is there something different in the silver process that makes it less adhesive to CLEAN glass?

Yes, me too, I don't need to silane glass before coating for mb-dcg.

For silver halide, I think the acidity of the developer play an important role. Jeff can certainly gives more details.

Even for the chrome hardening, if I don't silaned the plate, gelatin "crisps" and fall off the plate.

By the way, in old paper (about Lippmann plates or collodion), I read nowhere they presubbed their plates, however, they use acid developers (pyrogallol and al.)

In a old post, Martin pointed that some coat the plates with a very thin layer (small % of gelatin) of around 1 micron. Maybe not applicable here because the diffusion method load the "adhesive" layer to (just a thought)

posts.author: Sergio
posts.content_md:
AH, the A-1100 amino-silane, we use it with glass microscopic slides, it contains a natural humidity, water in the 0.1% range that will hydrolize the amino silane, this is the reaction necessary to bond to the glass, it really worth and works well, a very economic wip will do, it will keep safe and long on the original bottle.

The MSDS is available here: [http://www.hisglassworks.com/files/a1100msds.pdf](http://www.hisglassworks.com/files/a1100msds.pdf)

posts.content_md:
> **jean:** Yes, me too, I don't need to silane glass before coating for mb-dcg.For silver halide, I think the acidity of the developer play an important role. Jeff can certainly gives more details.Even for the chrome hardening, if I don't silaned the plate, gelatin "crisps" and fall off the plate.By the way, in old paper (about Lippmann plates or collodion), I read nowhere they presubbed their plates, however, they use acid developers (pyrogallol and al.)In a old post, Martin pointed that some coat the plates with a very thin layer (small % of gelatin) of around 1 micron. Maybe not applicable here because the diffusion method load the "adhesive" layer to (just a thought)

Yes, subbing might be something to try: bathing the plates in a 1% gelatin solution + a small amount of chrome alum and have them dry vertically.

Or, another option to improve gelatin adhesion on glass would be using lower gelatin concentrations. Of course this suggests changes to the coating method. In that case bar coating might be more convenient. By the way, using low viscosity solutions, Mayer bars are not even mandatory since we found simple threaded rods produced pretty nice layers.

Lower gelatin concentrations would imply 2 - 10% gelatin solutions.

Moreover, the particular gelatin quality might be paramount. With Aldrich's 300 bloom I could do things that were impossible with say, cooking gelatin. I was amazed to see that stuff stick on untreated PET film - and it even surived the fairly alkaline Neutol development + EDTA bleaching.

Sorry, I was not quite accurate. Having had a look into my notes, I see the gelatin subbing solution was 0,25% (2,5g/L).

Regarding the amount of chrome alum I've seen various ratios recommended - from 0,25% to 10% of the weight of gelatin. I used the lower concentration and it worked fine.
